newsitem.title: USA: Florida governor puts pressure on Miami.
newsitem.headline: Florida governor puts pressure on Miami.

text.p: Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles said Tuesday he would not take over financial control of Miami but would appoint an emergency board of advisors to aid and prod the deficit-plauged city in solving its own woes.
"The state is not going to take over Miami," said the govornor, who had been widely expected to do so. "We feel that a partnership is critical."
Chiles said he would appoint the board by the end of next week, led by his budget director Bob Bradley and deputy director Gail Sittig.

The board will not have authority to override the Miami City Commission, but will review city books, make recommendations and keep in direct contact with Chiles, who could take more drastic steps if necessary.
Chiles' aide April Herrle described their role as using a "bully pulpit" to ensure city officials take the necessary steps.
"We're not contemplating a bailout at this time," Chiles said. "We do want to work with city officials."

The loaning of budget experts and appointment of a board were among many options open to Chiles once Miami City Manager Ed Marquez formally notified him that Miami met Florida's legal definition of a city in fiscal crisis.
Marquez did that late Monday, declaring, "It is simply a matter of time until we confirm, through our accounting records, that the city had a fund balance deficit for two consecutive years."

After Miami's former city manager and former finance director resigned in the fall to face criminal corruption charges, an interim manager discovered the city had a $68 million deficit for the fiscal year that began Oct 1.

The books were in chaos and the city, which chronically spent more than it took in, was owed millions of dollars in unpaid rents and fees. City inspectors fanned out Tuesday in search of scofflaws who owe an estimated $1 million in unpaid garbage collection fees.

Miami made a $10.8 million payment on its bonds Monday, leaving it with $45 million in cash. Revenue from property tax payments should keep the city operating until late February or March, but the city will run out of money unless it takes drastic and politically unpopular steps by then.
The City Commission is scheduled to vote Dec 12 on proposals to raise garbage and other fees by about $10 million, and city employees will vote the next day on wage concessions.

Last month the state advanced the city $22 million in sales tax revenues that otherwise would have been paid over six months. Chiles has since criticized the city for failing to act quickly enough to raise garbage fees and take other steps to close the budget gap permanently.
City officials have discussed and rejected the possibility of filing for bankruptcy under Chapter 9, something they could not do that without the governor's permisson.
Bradley said bondholders had expressed concerns that "the city would go into Chapter 9 bankruptcy precipitously."
Chiles gave assurances that would not happen and said he did not intend to let Miami's bonds default.

"We're not going to allow anything that we can do something about," Chiles said. "That would be a terrible thing to have happen. It would be a terrible thing for the city and a terrible thing for the state and I would think there would be a lot of steps taken before something like that would happen."
Bond traders said there had been no panic selling of Miami's bonds, because most are insured.
